title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, operating margin is sanity, and free cash flow after maintenance and growth capex is reality.
epigraph.author: Industrial Capital Allocation Maxim

web_blocks.html: A forensic audit from ASE's 2018 merger through FY2025 and 9M 2026 highlights four traits [1][4][5][11]. ASE pairs durable scale and sharp operating leverage with strong operating cash conversion. In 2026, however, debt-funded AI CapEx turned free cash flow deeply negative [1][4]. Between FY2018 and FY2025, consolidated revenue grew from NT$371,088 million to NT$645,388 million (8.2% CAGR) [11]. In 9M 2026, revenue reached NT$608,887 million (+30.3% YoY), led by Q3 revenue of NT$244,161 million (nearly NT$977 billion annualized) [1][28]. Q3 parent net income hit NT$26,996 million. That lifted 9M 2026 net income to NT$62,193 million, topping all of FY2025 (NT$40,658 million) [1][5][28].

web_blocks.caption: ASE Technology Holding: Multi-Year Consolidated Financial Forensics (FY2018–FY2025 & Q3 2026, NT$ Million)
web_blocks.takeaway: ASE generated positive FCF every year from 2018 through 2024 before turning FCF-negative (-NT$19.9B in FY2025, or -NT$22.4B on a 20-F cash PP&E basis). 9M 2026 FCF then plunged to -NT$115,929M (-NT$75,390M in Q3 2026 alone) to finance its AI/LEAP cleanroom buildout [28][30].

web_blocks.html: Cash-conversion forensics reveal both a downturn buffer and severe capital drain during platform buildouts. In FY2023, ASE cut CapEx to NT$54,200 million while collecting NT$60B+ of depreciation. That lifted FCF to a record NT$60,222 million [4][11]. Across FY2019–FY2025, cumulative CFO reached NT$687,558 million against NT$274,349 million in parent net income (2.51x cash conversion) [4][11]. In 2025–2026, CapEx outpaced internal cash flow. Audited FY2025 PP&E payments totaled NT$164,643 million (NT$162,149 million net, FCF -NT$19,900 million) [4][30]. In 9M 2026, CFO climbed to NT$133,863 million, backed by NT$60,929 million of D&A (NT$22,258 million in Q3 alone) [1][28]. Net cash PP&E CapEx still surged to NT$249,792 million (NT$125,852 million in Q3). As a result, 9M 2026 FCF fell to -NT$115,929 million (-NT$75,390 million in Q3 2026) [1][28].

Updating balance-sheet forensics to September 30, 2026 exposes a steep leverage shift hidden by year-end 2025 numbers [1][4]. At year-end 2025, ASE held NT$92,469 million cash against NT$264,097 million debt (NT$171,628 million net debt) and paid NT$1,712 million net interest [4][30]. To fund 9M 2026's -NT$115,929 million FCF deficit plus NT$28,958 million in cash dividends, ASE raised NT$140,862 million in net new debt (NT$100,925 million in Q3) [1][28]. At Sep 30, 2026, cash stood at NT$88,421 million plus NT$19,517 million in current financial assets [29]. Total interest-bearing debt surged +53.9% to NT$406,461 million across NT$70,428M short-term debt, NT$5,141M current LT debt, NT$42,201M bonds, NT$276,633M LT bank loans, and leases [1][2][29]. Reported net debt-to-equity jumped from 0.47x (Q2) to 0.66x (Q3) [29]. Net interest expense climbed to NT$2,611 million in Q3 alone (NT$6,040 million in 9M 2026, already 3.5x FY2025) [1][28]. FY2025 Form 20-F footnotes flag three extra risks [4][30]. First, NT$155,178 million of LT debt matures in 1–3 years, including US$2,496.2M variable USD loans at 4.02% and NT$47.4B NT$ loans in 2027. A 100 bps rate rise adds NT$1,833 million/year on the 2025 base [4][30]. Second, unrecognized PP&E commitments reached NT$135,248 million (US$4.31B) at end-2025 (NT$114.7B unpaid), plus NT$16,480 million ROU lease assets at Sep 30, 2026 [1][4][30]. Third, Note 37(e) customer capacity deposits lifted non-current other liabilities from NT$7,057M (2024) to NT$37,585M (2025) and NT$109,152M total by Sep 30, 2026 [1][4][28][30]. Meanwhile, 9M 2026 non-operating income included NT$7,775 million in derivative and financial-asset valuation gains [28].

Capital-efficiency, minority-leakage, and governance metrics reinforce why ASE earns a conditional rather than unqualified compounder grade. Trailing ROIC sits near 10.28% (ROE 20.53%, ROA 7.28%), only modestly above an estimated 8%–9% WACC during the buildout, though Q3 2026's 13.6% operating margin is lifting near-term returns [1][4][13]. Share count stayed disciplined at ~2.21 billion ADS equivalent (~4.53 billion diluted underlying shares in Q3 2026), with minor dilution from convertibles and options [28]. Post-cutoff Form 4 filings on Nov 13 and Nov 16, 2026 recorded routine 2018-grant option exercises (code M at NT$41.10/share) by GM Tien-Szu Chen (300,000 shares) and Director Andrew R. Tang (350,000 shares, holding 660,000 shares directly) with zero open-market sales [31][32]. Minority leakage remains modest at ~2.7% of 9M 2026 net income (NT$1,743 million) from public stakes in USI Shanghai [28]. Non-core real estate holdings include NT$3,710 million in Kunshan real-estate inventory and a NT$3,375 million equity stake in related-party Hung Ching Development [4][30]. SPIL also raised NT$16.194 billion in equity capital for AI packaging purchases (TrendForce, Aug 12, 2026), while quarterly D&A climbs toward ~NT$90B annualized [36]. The decisive 2027–2028 test is whether ASE's $11.5 billion CapEx wave earns >15% incremental ROIC without covenant strain.

web_blocks.title: Balance Sheet & Footnote Forensics Summary (Dec 31, 2025 vs. Sep 30, 2026)
paragraphs: Debt Surge & Interest Escalation (Q3 2026 6-K): Total interest-bearing debt rose +53.9% in 9M 2026 from NT$264,097M (Dec 2025) to NT$406,461M (Sep 30, 2026) against NT$88,421M cash plus NT$19,517M current financial assets [1][2][29]. Reported net debt-to-equity jumped from 0.47x (Q2 2026) to 0.66x (Q3 2026) [29]. Net interest expense hit NT$2,611M in Q3 2026 alone (NT$6,040M in 9M 2026 vs. NT$1,712M in all of FY2025) [1][28].

2027 Maturity Wall & Footnote Commitments (20-F): NT$155,178M of long-term debt matures in 1–3 years, including US$2,496.2M variable USD loans at 4.02% and NT$47.4B NT$ loans in 2027 [30]. Floating-rate sensitivity stands at NT$1,833M/year per 100 bps on the 2025 base [4][30]. Unpaid PP&E purchase commitments totaled NT$114,686M at end-2025 alongside NT$16,480M ROU lease assets at Sep 30, 2026 [1][4][30].

9M 2026 Cash Burn & Prepayment Cushion: 9M 2026 cash PP&E outlays of NT$249,792M swamped CFO of NT$133,863M, leaving -NT$115,929M FCF (-NT$75,390M in Q3 alone) [28]. Customer capacity prepayments under Note 37(e) lifted non-current other liabilities to NT$109,152M (from NT$37,585M at end-2025 and NT$7,057M at end-2024), partially offsetting borrowing needs [1][4][30].

book_paragraphs: Now let us put ASE Technology Holding's ten-year financial statements under the forensic microscope. When you step back and look at the numbers from 2018 through 2025, a fascinating pattern jumps off the page—one that completely changes how you think about cash flow in semiconductor manufacturing.

First, look at the growth and cyclicality of the income statement. When ASE and SPIL merged in 2018, consolidated revenue was NT$371 billion. By 2025, it reached NT$645 billion—and in the single third quarter of 2026 alone, ASE booked NT$244 billion, nearly a one-trillion-NT-dollar annualized run rate. Yet that climb was anything but a straight line. Revenue peaked at NT$671 billion in 2022 with NT$61.5 billion in parent net profit, then dropped thirteen percent in 2023 to NT$582 billion with net profit falling to NT$35.5 billion. Operating margins swung from 14.1 percent in 2021 down to 7.0 percent in 2024, and then surged right back to 13.6 percent in Q3 2026. If you own ASE, you are signing up for operating leverage that cuts both ways.

Second, look at the remarkable counter-cyclical stabilizer on the cash flow statement. Between 2019 and 2025, ASE generated NT$688 billion in cumulative operating cash flow against NT$274 billion in cumulative parent net income—converting earnings into operating cash at a 2.5-to-1 clip because of massive non-cash depreciation. Even more interesting is what happens in a downturn. In 2023, when semiconductor demand slumped and net profit fell to NT$35.5 billion, ASE simply tapped the brakes on new machinery purchases, cutting capex to NT$54.2 billion. Because depreciation kept rolling in, Free Cash Flow actually jumped to an all-time record of NT$60.2 billion in the middle of a recession year! Conversely, in 2025, when AI demand exploded, ASE doubled capex to NT$162.1 billion and turned Free Cash Flow negative by nearly NT$20 billion.

Third, and most importantly, updating the balance sheet from December 2025 to September 30, 2026 reveals a much steeper leverage shift than year-end numbers implied. At year-end 2025, ASE held NT$92.5 billion in cash against NT$264.1 billion in debt and paid just NT$1.7 billion in net interest. Nine months later, after spending NT$249.8 billion on property and equipment against NT$133.9 billion of operating cash flow—producing negative free cash flow of NT$115.9 billion, including negative NT$75.4 billion in Q3 2026 alone—ASE borrowed NT$140.9 billion net to bridge capex and dividends. By September 30, 2026, total interest-bearing debt had surged nearly fifty-four percent to NT$406.5 billion, net debt-to-equity climbed from 0.47 times in Q2 to 0.66 times in Q3, and quarterly net interest expense hit NT$2.6 billion in Q3 alone—an annualized pace above NT$10 billion. Dig into the FY2025 Form 20-F footnotes and you see why utilization in 2027 matters so much: NT$155.2 billion of long-term debt matures within one to three years, including roughly 2.5 billion U.S. dollars of floating-rate dollar loans at four percent due in 2027, while quarterly depreciation has already climbed to NT$22.3 billion ahead of the full 2026 capex wave.

So what is the bottom-line forensic verdict before we ever look at a stock chart? ASE's trailing Return on Invested Capital sits around 10.3 percent—healthy, but only a couple of percentage points above its cost of capital during transition years. With 11.5 billion dollars of capex slated for 2026, ASE is making the largest capital bet in its forty-two-year history. If LEAP keeps doubling and factories stay full, ROIC will expand sharply and the 2025–2026 free-cash-flow deficit will flip into a gusher of cash by 2028. If AI server digestion hits before those machines are depreciated, fixed costs will bite hard.

Take a moment to appreciate how cleanly this ten-year forensic picture resolves the debate between ASE bulls and bears. The bulls are right that ASE is no longer a sleepy, low-margin wirebonder: Q3 2026's 13.6 percent consolidated operating margin and 30.6 percent ATM gross margin prove that advanced packaging is structurally lifting unit profitability. At the same time, the bears have a legitimate point on capital intensity: you cannot spend NT$162 billion in 2025 and guide for 11.5 billion US dollars in 2026 without accepting negative near-term free cash flow and higher future depreciation charges. That is why, purely on business quality and financial forensics, ASE is a conditional cyclical compounder—a premier industrial franchise undergoing a genuine AI-driven upgrade, whose long-term return on invested capital will ultimately be decided by factory utilization in 2027 and 2028.

Footnote forensics also surface two subtle balance-sheet details worth watching. On the positive side, non-current other liabilities surged from NT$7.1 billion at end-2024 to NT$37.6 billion at end-2025 and NT$109.2 billion total by Q3 2026, driven heavily by customer advance payments under Note 37(e) to lock in AI packaging capacity—meaning hyperscalers are co-funding part of the buildout. On the cautionary side, 9M 2026 non-operating income benefited from NT$7.8 billion in derivative and financial-asset valuation gains that can reverse when currency swaps reset, while routine November 2026 Form 4 filings showed insider option exercises at NT$41.10 with zero open-market selling. The verdict on the balance sheet is clear: ASE is still investment-grade resilient today, but it is no longer lightly levered—it has placed a leveraged bet on sustained 2027 and 2028 AI cleanroom utilization.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The forensic lesson of Chapter 6 is counter-intuitive: in OSAT, downturns often produce peak Free Cash Flow (NT$60.2B in 2023) because capex stops faster than depreciation, whereas booms produce negative Free Cash Flow (-NT$19.9B in 2025) because you must build tomorrow's cleanrooms today. Judging ASE solely on 2025–2026 FCF without adjusting for growth capex misses the cycle—just as ignoring the $11.5B capital commitment misses the risk.
